newsitem.title: USA: Stern sees U.S. economic expansion continuing.
newsitem.headline: Stern sees U.S. economic expansion continuing.

text.p: Minneapolis Federal Reserve President Gary Stern said Tuesday he sees nothing on the horizon to knock the six-year old U.S. economic expansion off its current course.
Stern told a business group in Marquette, Mich., that the expansion has been "well balanced" and "well maintained."

"It seems to be a very sound expansion and I don't see much on the horizon that suggests we are going to get a change in economic performance any time soon," Stern said. "So, if I am right about that, the expansion ought to continue."
Stern also told the group that he did not believe a rise in the minimum wage will have a major impact on the economy.
"I am not of the view that the new minimum wage law is going to have major effects on the overall economy."
He said the rise comes at a time when the labor market is tight and few workers are actually working at the minimum wage.
He said inflation has remained under control despite a tight labor market and good level of economic growth. Historically such circumstances would have sparked a round of price increases.
"There have been pleasant surprises here, which has been all to the good," he said.
In his speech, Stern emphasized the importance for the Fed of achieving price stability as he reiterated themes from an article in the Minneapolis Fed's 1995 annual report.

"The reason the Federal Reserve and other central banks have committed to low inflation is an accumulation of evidence indicating that economies perform better in terms of growth, employment and improved living standards in a low inflation environment," Stern said.

The Minneapolis Fed chief said that maintaining low inflation helps to promote sustainable growth over the long term and can make the economy less vulnerable to shocks, such as big swings in asset prices.

"A low inflation economy is less likely to engender the sharp swings in asset prices and in expectations about such prices that have been so devastating to the financial system from time to time," Stern said.
